To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
aluminum and boron complexes of phosphonic acids and their derivatives are effective, two-component gelators of organic liquids.
complexes of phosphonic and bisphosphonic acids with aluminum(III), and of phosphonic acids with boron(III), are gelators for a wide variety of organic liquids.
complexes of phosphonates with Al, B, and Zr form gels in organic liquids at room temperature.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the synthesis of new gelators, the characterization of the gel structures, and the development of new gelation mechanisms.
the synthesis of phosphorus-containing amphipathic compounds, the formation of complexes with metal ions, the gelation of organic solvents, and the properties of the gelled materials.
the development of new gelators that are based on the spontaneous complexation of phosphorus-containing amphiles with ions of aluminum and boron.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
these phosphorus-containing compounds, which are latent gelators, can form gels in a wide variety of organic liquids upon complexation with Al(III) or B(III).
the gels are formed from complexes that have a structure that is different from that of the free components and that are not present in the liquid before gelation occurs.
the gels are made from complexes of the phosphorus-containing gelator with Al, which form spontaneously upon mixing the components at ambient conditions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the complexes of aluminum(III), boron(III), and zirconium(III) with phosphonic acid mono- and diesters are gelators of a variety of organic liquids.
we have found a new class of organogelators, the phosphonate-Al complexes, which form thermally reversible gels spontaneously upon mixing the components.
the gels were formed by the spontaneous complexation of the phosphorus-containing amphipathic compounds with the metal ions.
The main takeaway from our work is that

the formation of organogels from phosphorus-containing amphipathic molecules is a general phenomenon, and it is possible to design phosphorus-containing amphiles that gelate a variety of organic liquids.
it is possible to make a gelator from two freely flowing solutions that are mixed together at room temperature.

it is possible to make gels from a wide variety of liquids by complexation of a phosphorus-containing gelator with an appropriate metal ion, without the need to use a catalyst or to heat or irradiate the mixture.
